title: Fen and the Hidden Truth
markdown:
Once upon a time, in the high mountain provinces, cedars grew so tall their tops tickled the clouds, and slate roofs glinted like sleepy ravens’ wings after a spring thaw. The air smelled of pine needles and damp earth even on the clearest days. That was the home of Ogre Fen, who was not the grumbling sort from dusty tales but sturdy and decent, with eyes like pebbles smoothed by a thousand years of river flow. His companion was Kettle, a goat whose ears twitched at the slightest whisper of wind and whose grey fleece seemed to absorb the worries of the world.

Fen’s hardship was a simple one, and therefore difficult. He wished to be thought a proper guide: imposing, certain, a master of mist and path. He was, in truth, a mountain ogre who cared for his guests and sometimes tied his boots in a hurry.

One crisp morning, as snowmelt rivers chattered down the slopes, a shadow fell across his humble dwelling. Lord Aerion had come from the distant lowlands, robes a vibrant splash against the muted mountain palette, wishing to travel the formidable Cedar Peaks. Fen felt a flutter in his chest like a fledgling owl testing its wings. He smoothed his rough tunic of woven wool and puffed out his chest.

“Welcome, Lord Aerion,” Fen rumbled, aiming for calm authority. “It is a pleasure to have you. I shall guide you through these parts.” He gestured toward winding mist-veiled paths. Kettle, sensing the tremor in his hand, nudged his leg with a soft bleat that seemed to say they would manage.

They ventured into whispering pines and over moss-covered boulders. Fen pointed out the Watcher’s Rock that resembled a stern face, albeit with a slightly shaky finger, and assured Lord Aerion the path was perfectly safe even when the mist made familiar stones look like slumbering giants. Kettle trotted beside them, sure-footed, occasionally nibbling a succulent patch of moss. The scent of damp earth and decaying leaves filled the air, a perfume unique to those high places.

The first trial waited at a lonely shepherd’s hut of stones gathered from the surrounding hills. An ogre sat outside, whittling with slow deliberate strokes. This was Hywel, known for an observant nature that missed neither a misplaced feather nor a stray shadow nor the subtle shift in a person’s gait. He looked up, eyes small but piercing as obsidian chips.

“Fen,” Hywel grunted, his voice like stones grinding, a sound that made Kettle’s ears swivel. “You’ve got an extra pebble in your boot, looks like. And Lord Aerion there looks as if he’s forgotten to pack his compass, but his pockets are bulging with honeycomb.”

Fen’s stomach did a little flip. He had not even realised he had picked up a stray stone. The honeycomb he had given Lord Aerion earlier for energy. Hywel’s observations were far too precise for comfort. Fen gave a strained smile. “Just a bit of mountain grit. And the Lord enjoys a sweet treat now and then. Helps with the journey.” He nudged Kettle forward. “Onwards.”

The second trial came as they left Hywel’s earshot, though not his memory. Fen had been tending the mist. It was not merely weather. He had thickened it, a foolish painted backdrop, so the path would look more challenging than it was and Lord Aerion would think him master of treacherous peaks. The motif of the three trials was the same each time: something small and true that Fen would rather have kept in his pocket.

A magnificent sight parted the swirling mist like a silken curtain. A young dragon landed with a soft rustle of air, scales the colour of deep emeralds, wings like shimmering jade. This was Ignis, and to Fen’s astonishment he bowed his head with perfect grace.

“Good day, esteemed travellers,” Ignis said, his voice like the chime of ancient bells. “I hope I am not intruding. My mother advised me to practise my greetings in unfamiliar company. She believes politeness is the highest form of courage.”

Lord Aerion gasped. Fen, despite his unease, felt a flicker of admiration. “Impeccable manners,” he muttered.

The third trial was Ignis’s courtesy turned keen. The dragon tilted his great head, regal and curious. “Ogre Fen, your left boot appears to be untied. A potential hazard. And I perceive that the mist is not merely a natural phenomenon today, but a rather cleverly crafted illusion. Rather like a poorly painted backdrop on a stage, if I may be so bold.” He turned to Lord Aerion. “That pouch you clutch so tightly contains not a map, but a rather detailed itinerary of potential foraging spots, does it not? And the faint scent of dried lavender? A curious choice for mountain travel. I find it most intriguing.”

Fen felt a blush creep up his thick neck, a warmth he had not felt since he was a young ogreling hiding a stolen berry. The descent, the hardest trial, was simply standing there while the last of the pretence came loose. Lord Aerion’s research was more about rare herbs than ancient ruins, a passion for botany Fen had failed to appreciate. The pebble in the boot, the honeycomb, the untied lace, the stage-mist: each a small honesty Fen had tried to outwalk.

It was Kettle who saved the moment, as she so often did. She butted her head against Fen’s leg, then nudged a loose strap on his boot, as if to say they might as well be honest. Then she gave a series of soft knowing bleats, looking directly at Ignis.

Ignis understood. “My dear Lord,” he said, gentle but firm, “while your dedication to botanical discovery is admirable, Ogre Fen’s concern for your safety is paramount. He wishes to ensure your journey is without undue alarm, even if his methods are perhaps more direct than the average guide.” He looked at Fen, a silent understanding passing between them. “And Ogre Fen, your thoughtfulness in offering sustenance, like that most delicious honeycomb, is a virtue that shines brighter than any carefully constructed façade. It speaks of a truly generous spirit.”

Fen blinked. The warmth of those words and Kettle’s quiet nudging dissolved the last remnants of his pretence. “Lord Aerion,” he said, voice steady now, “the path ahead is indeed rough, but not impassable. And the mist: I confess I thought it might worry you unnecessarily. It was a foolish attempt to seem more in control than I felt. Kettle and Ignis have shown me that honesty is the surest footing. I am Fen, a mountain guide who cares for his guests, and I am sorry I tried to be something I am not.”

The pretence, which had been the only wrongdoer on that path, received its proportionate consequence: it was left behind on the pine needles, with no audience left to impress.

Lord Aerion smiled, a genuine warmth lighting his eyes. “And I, Fen, am a scholar who appreciates truth, even when it smells of lavender and honeycomb. It seems I have underestimated the mountain folk. Your honest hearts are more valuable than any carefully crafted illusion.”

There was a Ghibli pause then, because mountain paths allow such things. They sat on a sun-warmed slab and shared the last of the honeycomb while mist, now only weather, drifted through the cedars. A hawk called. Kettle chewed moss with diplomatic concentration. Ignis practised a smaller bow, as if even dragons needed a quiet rehearsal.

The rest of the journey was more relaxed, filled with comfortable silence and shared observations. Fen, guided by Kettle’s cues and Ignis’s polite remarks about a rare mountain flower or the distant call of a hawk, led Lord Aerion safely to the lowlands. The parting was warm, filled with promises to visit.

Back in the mountain province the news spread on the wind, but it was not the dragon’s magnificence or the scholar’s knowledge that the villagers kept. It was the story of Ogre Fen, who, when his pretence faltered, revealed a heart as sturdy as the ancient cedars. That evening lanterns glowed on wet cobblestones. There was simple stew, music on wooden flutes like wind through the peaks, and laughter in the crisp air. Fen sat with Kettle’s head on his knee and felt a quiet contentment settle, deep and warm.

He was not a fearsome ogre, nor a perfectly controlled guide. He was Fen, and that was enough. A true path asks less armour than a false one, and it still leads home; their tale is still told when the thaw shines the slate.
characters: Fen (sturdy mountain ogre), Kettle (a sharp-minded grey goat), Ignis (a young dragon with impeccable manners)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, highland fantasy adventure for teens
author: StoryGen Community
